title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, contamination‑check evidence (10% Mininet holdout → 20 tasks; contamination summary records zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages or policy violations. The generate–validate–repair (GVR) architecture—LLM generation followed by a deterministic validator and an optional automated repair step—aims to reduce such operational risk. However, the practical value of an automated repair step is conditional on (i) baseline validator‑detectable failure prevalence under the chosen generation policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study was sealed before any model calls (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).
sections.related_work: Prior work documents LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and domain‑specific brittleness; mitigation approaches include grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures [10.1007/s11704-026-60308-3; https://openalex.org/W4399803256; https://openalex.org/W4410125989]. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration synthesis but generally lack instrumented, production‑like, preregistered failure‑rate studies [https://openalex.org/W4399629579; https://openalex.org/W4403635865]. Red‑team and agent‑audit work show that tool descriptions and chainings change safety outcomes, motivating external validation and emulator checks [10.21203/rs.3.rs-10646209/v1; 10.2139/ssrn.7203631]. Our study situates itself among generator→validator→repair proposals by measuring a prespecified paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The study preregistration (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02; preregistration manifest hash: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one initial LLM generation per task (shared_initial semantics), and up to one automated repair call per task if the deterministic validator reported violations. The single primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes; 95% CIs used a paired bootstrap percentile method with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The primary estimand was the absolute paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and a target ≥50% relative reduction; the sample size n = 200 was selected accordingly.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across baseline and guarded conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. The hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) was invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); zero repair calls were consumed. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm provider accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, and all consistency checks passed. Primary validator outcomes. The primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) marked every initial candidate as valid: baseline_successes = 200/200, guarded_successes = 200/200; paired contingency table entries are n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Inferential statistics. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). No preregistered secondary estimands involving repair iterations or repair cost are reportable because no repairs occurred.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and conditionality. The degenerate confirmatory outcome—zero baseline validator failures—shows a simple logical point: when the chosen model, prompt template, and generation policy produce validator‑passing candidates for all items in a workload, an automated validator+repair step has no validator‑detectable failures to reduce. This does not imply that GVR is never useful; rather, GVR’s marginal operational value depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator fidelity. Why baseline failures were zero. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) the shared_initial deterministic sampling policy and the prompt template resulted in generator outputs that precisely matched the task‑encoded required_sequence; (2) the curated task bank encodes explicit workflow constraints that map directly to deterministic validator checks and may therefore be easier for a properly engineered prompt to satisfy; (3) the primary validator verifies the task‑encoded syntactic/intent constraints but may omit some device‑level behaviors observable only under end‑to‑end emulation or real devices; and (4) the single‑repair budget and shared_initial design removed per‑condition re‑sampling as a pathway for generating alternative, repairable candidates.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable because the baseline failure rate was 0% on this task bank. The operational lesson is that automated repair produces measurable benefit only when baseline validator failures are non‑negligible or when validator coverage is sufficient to detect common failure modes. Future studies should (a) evaluate workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, (b) expand validator fidelity with richer emulator or device semantics, (c) assess multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and (d) consider multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical gains.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02. Models and orchestration: the hosted model declared and used was gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics (one deterministic initial candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded conditions). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls (preregistration manifest hash: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6). Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and an artifact manifest are archived. Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) reporting zero disagreements. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) as required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.
Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised.
